# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

A reusable inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable dose of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and automatically rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose. The valve has a cylindrical housing with an inlet at one axial end and an outlet at the opposite axial end. A metering sleeve is fixed inside the housing. The sleeve defines a cylindrical dose chamber, a radial concentrate port, a carrier-liquid admission port, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber.

A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has two axially spaced sealing lands joined by a reduced-diameter waist. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while both lands isolate the carrier-liquid path. Movement to the discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port. Carrier liquid then enters behind the measured volume and expels that volume through a one-way outlet valve into the main flow. The ordering of the port edges and lands prevents the concentrate source from communicating directly with the carrier-liquid inlet.

An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod. Each full piston stroke turns the index collar by one increment. Three selectable axial stop faces on the collar set three dose volumes by limiting piston travel. A spring-biased detent engages one of three recesses to retain the selected setting. A transparent window in the housing shows one of three reference numerals carried on the collar, so the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics.

When the piston returns toward the fill position, a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land first wipes the dose-chamber wall. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass. Carrier liquid flows through an annular rinse channel between the sleeve and housing, through two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve, and then through the flush bypass to the outlet. The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. A replaceable cartridge contains the piston, metering sleeve, one-way outlet valve, and flush poppet and is retained by a threaded end cap. Removing the end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the housing connections. An apparatus claim and a method claim should cover the ordered isolation, metering, discharge, and automatic rinse sequence.

1	In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.
4	
5	The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.
6	
7	FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.
8	
9	The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.
10	
11	A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.
12	
13	In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.
14	
15	Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.
16	
17	The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.
18	
19	FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26.
20	
21	The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.
22	
23	The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.
24	
25	The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.
26	
27	The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.
28	
29	Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.
30	
31	FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.
32	
33	The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.
34	
35	The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.
36	
37	The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.
38	
39	The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.
40	
41	In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.
42	
43	The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.
44	
45	The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

1	Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly coloured, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurised carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.
4	
5	The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallises, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.
6	
7	Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.
8	
9	There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.
10

Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly coloured, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurised carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallises, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

file.content:
An inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable measured volume of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose, without any command additional to the stroke that delivers the dose.

The valve has a housing with an inlet and an outlet and a metering sleeve fixed within the housing. The metering sleeve defines a dose chamber, a concentrate port opening into the dose chamber, a carrier-liquid admission port opening into the dose chamber, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber. A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has an upstream sealing land and a downstream sealing land axially spaced from one another and joined by a reduced-diameter waist.

Separation of the two liquids is enforced by the axial order of the land faces and the port edges rather than by the sequence in which any external command arrives. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while the upstream and downstream sealing lands isolate the carrier-liquid admission port from the concentrate port. Movement of the piston toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port. Carrier liquid then enters behind the measured volume of concentrate and expels that volume through a one-way outlet valve toward the outlet. Because one land face has passed the concentrate port before the other land face releases the carrier-liquid admission port, no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path.

The rinse is carried out by the return of the same piston. An annular rinse channel lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve and an inner surface of the housing, and at least one rinse opening leads from that channel through the metering sleeve into the dose chamber. A follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass during the return stroke, so that carrier liquid sweeps the annular rinse channel, issues from the rinse opening across the surfaces wetted by the concentrate, and leaves through the flush bypass to the outlet. The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port to the dose chamber, so the rinse is complete, and the rinse liquid is on its way to the outlet, before any further concentrate can enter. The rinse cannot be omitted, mistimed or deferred, because the element that opens it is carried by the piston rod itself.

In described embodiments, a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land wipes the wall of the dose chamber before the flush poppet opens. Two radial rinse openings are directed across the concentrate port and across the one-way outlet valve.

Dose selection is mechanical and self-indexing. An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by the follower pin, so that each full stroke of the piston turns the index collar by one increment. Three selectable axial stop faces on the index collar limit the travel of the piston and thereby set three dose volumes, a spring-biased detent engaging one of three recesses retains the selected setting, and a transparent window in the housing shows one of three dose setting numerals carried by the index collar, so that the setting is visible without electronics.

A replaceable cartridge contains the piston, the metering sleeve, the one-way outlet valve and the flush poppet, and is retained by a threaded end cap. Removing the threaded end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the connections at the inlet and the outlet.

A corresponding method admits concentrate to the dose chamber, closes the concentrate port before uncovering the carrier-liquid admission port, expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve, and then opens the flush poppet with the follower pin during the return of the piston and closes it again before the concentrate port is reconnected.

input.summary: The application body was already complete and, per the reviewer's own source ledger, fully traced to the inventor text, so I changed nothing in the title, field, background, summary, claims, abstract or numeral table. I corrected the three internal-consistency defects the reviewer identified, plus one cross-figure consequence of the second fix. (1) FIG. 4 no longer places the metering sleeve's left end outside the index collar: the collar now extends leftward past that end, with the sleeve's hidden outline in broken line, so the follower pin 44 sits at the same axial station in FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 and can be simultaneously engaged in the cam groove and bearing on the poppet stem. I also extended the poppet stem in FIG. 3 leftward past the sleeve's left end so it actually reaches the pin. (2) In FIG. 3 the left radial rinse opening 62 moved off the station covered by the upstream sealing land to a station just downstream of the piston, clear of both lands and aimed up and left toward the concentrate port, so the depicted rinse jet has an open path onward to the flush bypass. Because that same opening appears unnumbered in FIG. 2, I moved it there too, from beneath the concentrate port to right of the downstream sealing land, so the two sections do not put one opening at two axial stations. (3) The FIG. 3 paragraph of the detailed description now introduces "a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36" with an indefinite article, and the FIG. 4 paragraph refers back to "the follower pin 44". One note on the record: the brief states that no prior-art search was run, and prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the art available to this draft may be incomplete and the Background contains no citations. No claim scope, no numeral, and no disclosed structure was altered.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries two features that do real technical work and that the specification explains as solving stated problems: the axial ordering by which the concentrate port is shut before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so separation is a property of the moving geometry rather than of command sequencing; and the flush poppet opened by the follower pin on the piston rod during the return stroke, closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse is an unavoidable part of the same stroke. With no reference listed in prior_art/INDEX.md, those are the features an argument would be built from, and both are stated in the specification in the same words as in the claim.

Left out of claim 1 deliberately: the index collar, the cam groove, the three stop faces, the detent, the window and the numerals, the flexible lip, the two-opening rinse arrangement, the cartridge and end cap, and the cylindrical housing with end-to-end ports. Each is a real fallback and each sits in a dependent claim (2, 3, 6 to 12), so claim 1 keeps only the ordered isolation and the stroke-driven rinse, which is the narrowest set that still makes the invention work.

The rinse channel and at least one rinse opening stay in claim 1 because the flush path recited in the last wherein clause needs antecedent structure to flow through; the count of rinse openings and their aiming is left to claim 2 so claim 1 is not limited to two.

Claims 4, 5 and 16 restate the disclosed ordering and the closed-port interval as separate positive limitations, so that if the wherein clauses of claim 1 are read as functional there is an express structural or timing fallback to retreat to.
The method claims 13 to 20 mirror the apparatus ladder because a valve maker and a valve user are different infringers, and the disclosure expressly asked for both classes.

On the drawings: the reviewer's finding that FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 put pin 44 on opposite sides of the sleeve's left end was correct, and the cure had to be on the FIG. 4 side, because FIG. 3's pin position is fixed by its need to reach the poppet stem. Extending the collar leftward over the sleeve end is a depiction arrangement only; it was not added to the description or the claims, and the description still says only that the index collar surrounds the metering sleeve.

On the left rinse opening: the disclosure fixes the timing (poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port), which means the upstream land necessarily overlies the concentrate port while the rinse runs. So the opening beneath that port could not be the one shown flowing, and only a station downstream of both lands has a path to the flush bypass. I moved the drawn station and kept the disclosed direction of the jet across the concentrate port, rather than touching the timing, which is inventor text.

I moved the same opening in FIG. 2 as well. The reviewer did not raise it, but leaving FIG. 2 with that opening beneath the concentrate port would have put one physical opening at two different axial stations in two sections of the same valve, which is the same class of defect the review had just found.

View: fragmentary side view of the index collar and the parts that set and retain the dose, collar axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The index collar is drawn as a cylindrical ring seen from the side in the middle of the drawing area: a long horizontal body, its left end closed by a shallow curved edge indicating the round section. It surrounds an unnumbered tube whose left end lies within the collar, the collar extending leftward beyond that end, the tube's hidden outline drawn in broken line.
- A helical cam groove is drawn on the visible cylindrical surface as a narrow band running from the lower left of that surface to the upper right, curving as it wraps around the body.
- A piston rod is drawn as a plain horizontal shaft entering the view from the left on the collar axis and ending within the left part of the collar surface. A short follower pin projects radially from the end of the shaft, its outer end sitting within the narrow band of the groove.
- The right end of the collar is stepped: its end face is divided into three faces at three different axial positions, drawn as three steps of increasing projection rightward, so that the face presented stands nearer to or further from an approaching part. These are the three axial stop faces.
- Three detent recesses lie at one station along the collar's length, at three angular positions about it. One is drawn as a rounded notch broken into the upper outline; the other two are drawn in broken line on the curved surface below it.
- Above the collar, a spring-biased detent is shown schematically as a small ball resting in the notch broken into the upper outline, and a short coil spring above the ball, the spring shown broken off at its upper end.
- Three dose setting numerals lie at one station along the collar's length, at three angular positions about it, drawn as small plain rectangular patches, the middle one full on the visible cylindrical surface and the other two curving away toward the upper and lower silhouettes. They are shown schematically and carry no drawing text.

Numerals on this sheet: 36, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54.

Targets:

- 36: the plain horizontal shaft entering the view from the left.
- 40: the visible cylindrical surface of the collar, well inside its outline and clear of the groove band.
- 42: the interior of the groove band, away from the follower pin.
- 44: the short pin projecting radially from the end of the shaft.
- 46: the middle one of the three stepped end faces at the right end.
- 48: the small ball resting in the notch.
- 50: the notch broken into the upper outline.
- 54: the patch full on the visible surface.

input.summary: The only failing mechanical check was brief length: FIG. 3 measured 2906 characters and FIG. 4 measured 2886, against a maximum of 2800. I shortened both briefs by removing invented rendering constraints and redundant phrasing, leaving every disclosed body, opening, contact, flow path and numeral target intact. FIG. 3 keeps the housing and sleeve bands, the annular rinse channel open at both ends, the flush bypass with its conical seat, the poppet head standing clear of that seat with its stem running past the sleeve's left end to the pin, the two-land piston with its shaft and upward pin, the flexible lip, the concentrate port covered by the left land, both radial rinse openings with the left one clear of the piston and aimed toward the concentrate port, and the covered unnumbered opening at the right land. FIG. 4 keeps the collar surrounding the tube with the collar extending leftward past the tube's left end, the helical groove band, the piston rod and follower pin engaged in that band, the three stepped end faces, the three detent recesses, the ball and coil spring, and the three schematic patches carrying no drawing text. What went is padding: sheet-edge phrasing beyond the drawing-area statement, "at the top and bottom" for the housing bands, a duplicated description of the housing interior that leads to the outlet, "a visible gap between them" where the head is already said to stand clear of its seat, the prescription of straight upper and lower collar outlines, and the invented vertical placement of the two hidden detent recesses. Two leader targets were also broadened rather than trimmed only for length: numeral 28 now names a broad interior of the piston instead of an outside-the-outline leader endpoint, and numeral 46 reads "the middle one of the three stepped end faces". No claim, description, numeral definition, drawing description or disclosed embodiment changed, and the per-sheet numeral lists are identical to before.
reasoning: The gate reported a single class of defect, brief length, so I confined the work to figures/FIG-3.md and figures/FIG-4.md and left the application text, the numeral table and draft/07 untouched. FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 were not flagged and were not edited.

I cut from the two categories the drafting rules already treat as removable: generic linework controls and placement constraints with no source in the disclosure. The collar's 'straight upper and lower outlines' is a renderer instruction, not invention geometry, and the vertical positions given for the two broken-line detent recesses ('one part way down and one near the lower outline') were invented to control the render. Neither carries any disclosed relationship.

Where a relationship was stated twice I kept one statement. The flush bypass bullet no longer repeats 'the housing interior that leads to the outlet' because the preceding bullet already establishes it, and the poppet head no longer both 'stands clear to the left of the seat' and has 'a visible gap between them'; the open condition is still expressly drawn.

Target 28 was the largest single saving and also the better target under the endpoint rule: a leader ending outside the outline with a specified arrowhead is an aesthetic coordinate, while a broad interior of the left enlarged portion identifies the piston unambiguously, since neither sealing land carries a numeral on this sheet.
Target 46 was reworded to 'the middle one of the three stepped end faces' so the position is read as a stable middle rather than as an ordinal whose counting direction could go either way.

I preserved the two fixes made for the earlier review, because they resolve findings the gate has already accepted: the collar in FIG. 4 still extends leftward beyond the tube's left end with the tube's hidden outline in broken line, keeping follower pin 44 at one axial station across FIG. 3 and FIG. 4, and the left rinse opening 62 in FIG. 3 still lies clear of both piston portions so its jet has an open path to the flush bypass.

Measured after the edit, FIG. 3 is 2781 bytes and FIG. 4 is 2773 bytes as whole files, and about 2705 and 2697 once the trailing numeral list is discounted, so both clear 2800 under either reading of the check.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

A cam groove is expressly a functional feature for which runout direction is substantive even when the brief calls the geometry schematic; the hand of the helix determines the sense in which each stroke indexes the collar. The source discloses the groove and the fact of one-increment-per-stroke indexing, but not its direction.

# FIG. 1

View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched wall bands that run across most of the view, joined at the right by a hatched end wall. The interior between them is open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth, its outer surface meeting the housing bore along a shallow saw-tooth interface indicating a thread. A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the body, out of the left end of the sleeve bore, and ends short of the end cap.
- A short tubular stub projects axially leftward from the left end of the housing below the axis, clear of the end cap and the shaft, and opens into the interior; it is the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects axially rightward from the end wall at the right and opens into the interior; it is the outlet, shown schematically. Both stubs end clear of the drawing area.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis, drawn as an upper hatched band and a lower hatched band spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it over part of its length, from a position right of the end cap to the right-hand end of the sleeve, which stands short of the end wall, the gap opening at that end into the housing interior that leads to the outlet.
- The sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry are drawn as one removable unit, the sleeve's left end standing within the left mouth of the housing short of the end cap; this unit is the cartridge.
- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, with the plain shaft running leftward from it.
- A rectangular unhatched panel is set into the upper housing wall band about midway along it, the hatching stopping at its outline; it is the transparent window. Beneath it, on an unnumbered ring surrounding the sleeve in the gap, a small plain patch shows.

Numerals on this sheet: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66.

- 66: the hatched ring in the left mouth of the housing.

lines: The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

-FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 and holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26.

+FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.
The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched wall bands that run across most of the view, joined at the right by a hatched end wall. The interior between them is open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth, meeting the housing bore along a shallow saw-tooth interface indicating a thread. 17	The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.
18	
19	FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.
20	
21	The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.
22	
23	The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.
24	
25	The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.
26	
27	The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.
28	
29	Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

input.summary: Every listed item is fixed, and all of the substantive fixes are deletions or genericising rewrites inside figures/; no claim, description sentence, numeral definition or embodiment was widened to accommodate a drawing. The seven critical items: the annular rinse channel no longer has open ends into the housing interior in FIG. 1 or FIG. 3, leaving the single disclosed flush route of channel, rinse openings, flush bypass, outlet; the one-way outlet valve is now a plain closure element across a passage in FIG. 2 and FIG. 3, with no seat taper or contact topology, and target 38 follows; the flush poppet is a plain closure element standing clear of the passage mouth and joined by a plain stem to the follower pin, with the conical head, conical seat, seat location and the stem route through the rinse channel all deleted; the cam groove is a narrow band wrapping the body with hand and pitch not indicated; the stop faces are three faces at three axial positions on one stepped end face, with the ordering not indicated and target 46 reading "one of the three stepped end faces"; the numbered rinse opening no longer carries an axial position relative to the lands or an aim angle, so the incoherent blocked jet is gone; and the flexible lip is a thin flexible projection contacting each bore wall, with flare direction not indicated. The two major items: FIG. 1 now puts the unnumbered ring in the left length of the annulus with its left part beyond the sleeve's left end, where FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 put the follower pin, limits the clear gap to the length of the annulus right of that ring, and sets the transparent window above the ring so the window still shows a numeral carried on the collar; and the piston rod is broken off at a conventional break line short of the end cap, asserting neither a blind end nor a cap penetration. The four minor items: the concentrate connection is a short stub broken off within the view in both FIG. 2 and FIG. 3; the detent is a plain detent element seated in a plain recess with a spring behind it shown broken off, with targets 48 and 50 following; numerals.md rows 46, 50, 54 and 62 are singular; and claim 9 now recites "one of the three dose setting numerals" associated with "a selected one of the three selectable axial stop faces", curing both singular terms. On numeral 36 and FIG. 3: the sheet already carries the maximum of eight numerals, so instead of a ninth the description's FIG. 3 recitation no longer states that the piston rod 36 is shown there, and a following sentence states that the follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36; the pin keeps its indefinite first mention and the rod stays labelled on FIG. 4. All four briefs were also trimmed back under the 2800 character cap that the previous gate enforced.
reasoning: Every critical item was an assertion about a functional surface that the disclosure does not describe, so each was cured by deleting the assertion and leaving the least specific outline that still shows the disclosed function: a plain closure element for both the one-way outlet valve and the flush poppet, a plain recess and a plain detent element, a groove band without hand, and a lip without flare direction. Nothing about the invention was narrowed, because none of these forms ever appeared in the claims, the summary or the detailed description.

The rinse channel fix mattered most for the invention rather than for the drawing: an annulus open at both ends into the housing interior would have depicted a permanent bypass around the sleeve, which would undercut the very feature claim 1 rests on, namely that carrier liquid reaches the outlet through the flush bypass only when the follower pin holds the poppet open. Removing the open ends restores the single ordered path the disclosure gives.

For the collar, the constraint was that the disclosure puts both the index collar and the annular rinse channel between the sleeve and the housing, while the follower pin must reach the groove from the piston rod. I put the ring in the left length of the annulus, where FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 already place the pin, and limited the rinse gap to the length right of it. The window moved to sit above the ring rather than midway, because the window must show a numeral carried on the collar; keeping it midway would have separated it from the collar it reads.

The piston rod break line was chosen over either alternative on purpose. The source says nothing about how the rod is driven or whether it leaves the housing, so a blind end contradicts the description's driven stroke while a cap penetration would invent a seal and a drive path. A conventional break line asserts neither and is silent in the way the source is silent.

On numeral 36, the reviewer's suggested cure would have made nine numerals on FIG. 3, one over the per sheet maximum, and every numeral on that sheet is needed there: 26, 56, 58, 60 and 62 appear nowhere else, 28 is the piston as a whole, and 22 anchors the rinse opening that is directed across it. So I removed the assertion instead of adding the label, by taking 36 out of the FIG. 3 recitation sentence and stating the rod relationship in a following sentence of body text. The pin still gets its indefinite first mention in the FIG. 3 paragraph, which is what the earlier antecedent fix required.

Claim 9 was redrafted rather than patched with an article, because both singular terms lacked antecedents and claim 7 supplies the plural set: the window now shows one of the three dose setting numerals, and that one is tied to a selected one of the three selectable axial stop faces. The detailed description already says exactly this, so no support was added.

The singular numeral table entries were taken because each leader lands on one member of a group. The description still reads three axial stop faces 46, three detent recesses 50, three dose setting numerals 54 and two radial rinse openings 62, which remains correct with a singular part name in the table and keeps one meaning per numeral.

Length had to be managed while making these edits, since the previous gate rejected FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 for exceeding 2800 characters and the genericising rewrites added words. I recovered the space from invented rendering constraints rather than from geometry: sheet-edge clauses beyond the drawing-area statement, a restated explanation of a break line, and over-specified leader endpoints such as the FIG. 1 numeral 10 leader ending just outside the housing outline, which is now a broad interior target on the upper housing wall band.

Nothing in this turn touched the shape of the claimed combination. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed again before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. The rinse channel fix mattered most for the invention rather than for the drawing: an annulus open at both ends into the housing interior would have depicted a permanent bypass around the sleeve, which would undercut the very feature claim 1 rests on, namely that carrier liquid reaches the outlet through the flush bypass only when the follower pin holds the poppet open. Removing the open ends restores the single ordered path the disclosure gives.

For the collar, the constraint was that the disclosure puts both the index collar and the annular rinse channel between the sleeve and the housing, while the follower pin must reach the groove from the piston rod. I put the ring in the left length of the annulus, where FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 already place the pin, and limited the rinse gap to the length right of it. The window moved to sit above the ring rather than midway, because the window must show a numeral carried on the collar; keeping it midway would have separated it from the collar it reads.

The piston rod break line was chosen over either alternative on purpose. The source says nothing about how the rod is driven or whether it leaves the housing, so a blind end contradicts the description's driven stroke while a cap penetration would invent a seal and a drive path. A conventional break line asserts neither and is silent in the way the source is silent.

On numeral 36, the reviewer's suggested cure would have made nine numerals on FIG. 3, one over the per sheet maximum, and every numeral on that sheet is needed there: 26, 56, 58, 60 and 62 appear nowhere else, 28 is the piston as a whole, and 22 anchors the rinse opening that is directed across it. So I removed the assertion instead of adding the label, by taking 36 out of the FIG. 3 recitation sentence and stating the rod relationship in a following sentence of body text. The pin still gets its indefinite first mention in the FIG. 3 paragraph, which is what the earlier antecedent fix required.

Claim 9 was redrafted rather than patched with an article, because both singular terms lacked antecedents and claim 7 supplies the plural set: the window now shows one of the three dose setting numerals, and that one is tied to a selected one of the three selectable axial stop faces. The detailed description already says exactly this, so no support was added.

The singular numeral table entries were taken because each leader lands on one member of a group. The description still reads three axial stop faces 46, three detent recesses 50, three dose setting numerals 54 and two radial rinse openings 62, which remains correct with a singular part name in the table and keeps one meaning per numeral.

Length had to be managed while making these edits, since the previous gate rejected FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 for exceeding 2800 characters and the genericising rewrites added words. I recovered the space from invented rendering constraints rather than from geometry: sheet-edge clauses beyond the drawing-area statement, a restated explanation of a break line, and over-specified leader endpoints such as the FIG. 1 numeral 10 leader ending just outside the housing outline, which is now a broad interior target on the upper housing wall band.

# FIG. 1

View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched wall bands that run across most of the view, joined at the right by a hatched end wall. The interior between them is open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth, meeting the housing bore along a shallow saw-tooth interface indicating a thread. A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the body, out of the left end of the sleeve bore, and is broken off at a conventional break line short of the end cap.
- A short tubular stub projects axially leftward from the left end of the housing below the axis, clear of the end cap and the shaft, and opens into the interior; it is the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects axially rightward from the end wall at the right and opens into the interior; it is the outlet, shown schematically. Both stubs end well inside the drawing area.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis, drawn as an upper hatched band and a lower hatched band spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it over the portion of its length right of the ring described below.
- The sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry are drawn as one removable unit, the sleeve's left end standing within the left mouth of the housing short of the end cap; this unit is the cartridge.
- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, with the plain shaft running leftward from it.
- An unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve in the annulus over the left portion of its length, its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end, clear of that gap.
- A rectangular unhatched panel is set into the upper housing wall band above the ring, the hatching stopping at its outline; it is the transparent window. On the ring beneath the panel a small plain patch shows.

Numerals on this sheet: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66.

# FIG. 2

View: enlarged longitudinal sectional view of the metering portion of FIG. 1, axis horizontal, with the piston in the fill position. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The metering sleeve is cut lengthwise on its axis and appears as upper and lower hatched wall bands running across the width of the view. The open space between them is the cylindrical dose chamber.
- An outer housing wall appears in section as hatched bands above and below the sleeve bands, each spaced outward so that a clear gap runs above and below the sleeve.
- In the left portion of the dose chamber, an upstream sealing land is drawn as a hatched block whose upper and lower edges meet the bore walls, a downstream sealing land as a second such block spaced to its right, and a waist joining them as a hatched bar of smaller height on the axis, so that open space is visible between the waist and each bore wall.
- A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the upstream sealing land and is broken off within the view.
- A radial opening passes through the upper sleeve band between the two sealing lands, its inner mouth opening into the space above the waist; this is the concentrate port. - A second opening passes through the lower sleeve band at the downstream sealing land, its inner mouth covered by that land and its outer mouth opening into the clear gap below the sleeve. This is the carrier-liquid admission port, right of the concentrate port.

# FIG. 3

View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- An outer housing wall appears in section as upper and lower hatched bands. Inside it the sleeve wall appears as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward; between them is the bore.
- The clear gap between the sleeve and outer bands, above and below, is the annular rinse channel, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end; its ends are not shown open to the housing interior.
- Toward the right a passage leads from the bore up through the upper sleeve band toward the outlet: the flush bypass. A plain closure element stands clear of the mouth of that passage and is connected by a plain stem to the follower pin; both are shown schematically without seat or contact detail and are the flush poppet.
- In the bore, in the left half, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion. A plain shaft extends leftward on the axis past the sleeve's left end, and a short pin projects from it to the stem, holding the closure element clear of the passage mouth.
- A thin flexible projection extends from the left portion into contact with the upper bore wall and a matching one into contact with the lower bore wall: the flexible lip, shown schematically without flare direction.
- An opening through the upper sleeve band, covered by the left portion, is the concentrate port, with a short stub rising from it, broken off in the view.
- Between the piston and the flush bypass a further passage leads from the bore up through the upper sleeve band, with a plain closure element drawn across it, shown schematically: the one-way outlet valve, unnumbered.
- Two openings through the lower sleeve band connect the rinse channel to the bore: the radial rinse openings. The left one faces the concentrate port and is shown directed across it; the right one faces the one-way outlet valve passage and is shown directed across it. Their positions relative to the piston are not otherwise indicated.
- A further opening through the lower sleeve band at the right portion of the piston is covered by it; unnumbered.

Numerals on this sheet: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62.

input.summary: All eight findings are fixed, seven inside figures/ and one in the description. The two critical disclosure-fidelity items: the carrier-liquid admission port no longer opens into the annulus that FIG. 3 designates the annular rinse channel, its outer mouth being broken off at a conventional break line within the lower sleeve band in FIG. 2, with the matching break added to the covered lower opening in FIG. 3, so no feed connection between the admission path and the rinse channel is asserted; and the flush poppet no longer has a permanent linkage to the follower pin, the closure element now carrying a plain stem whose free end is abutted by the pin in this view, which matches the description's statement that the pin reaches the poppet and opens it near the end of the return stroke. The four major items: FIG. 1 numeral 10 now reaches the assembly by an arrowed lead line touching the outer contour of the housing at the upper right while 12 takes the upper housing wall band and the lower band is left unnumbered; numeral 64 now touches the left end face of the sleeve where it stands in the left mouth of the housing, clear of the bands targeted by 18; the annular rinse channel in FIG. 3 is open at the left toward the inlet end of the housing with its right end closed by the sleeve meeting the housing wall, so the supply path recited in the description, the summary and claim 1 is traceable in the figure; and "over part of its length" is deleted from the sleeve spacing sentence in the detailed description. The two minor items: the left radial rinse opening in FIG. 3 now lies immediately right of the left enlarged portion with its inner mouth open to the bore and directed toward the concentrate port, so nothing covers it; and numeral 28 reaches the piston as a whole by an arrowed lead line touching its lower outline where the middle portion meets the right enlarged portion, instead of landing on the block that FIG. 2 numbers 30. FIG. 2's unnumbered lower openings moved to the same axial station the FIG. 3 fix uses, so one opening is not drawn at two stations across the two sections. All four briefs were retrimmed to stay under the 2800 character cap; the space came from redundant phrasing such as a repeated statement that the stubs end inside the drawing area, not from geometry or relationships.
reasoning: The two critical items were both flow-topology assertions, and each was cured by removing the assertion rather than by adding structure. Showing the admission port's outer mouth broken off leaves the figure silent on where the port draws from, which is where the disclosure is silent, and it prevents the drawing from implying that the rinse channel feeds the metering charge, a path that would sit under the control of the flush poppet and would change what the valve does.

The poppet stem was the more consequential of the two. A permanent stem linkage would mean the follower pin governs the poppet throughout every stroke, which contradicts the disclosed timing that the poppet is normally closed and is opened near the end of the return stroke, and that timing is what claim 1 rests on. Making the stem a member of the poppet that the pin merely abuts in this one view keeps the depicted contact without asserting a permanent connection.

The rinse channel had to be opened at the inlet end rather than left closed at both ends, because the description, the summary and claim 1 all recite carrier liquid flowing through the channel, and the inlet is the only carrier-liquid source the disclosure gives. Closing the right end at the sleeve-to-housing junction keeps the single ordered route of channel, rinse openings, flush bypass, outlet, and does not reopen the permanent bypass that an earlier pass removed.

For numerals 10 and 12 and for 18 and 64, the problem was that a whole-assembly numeral and a component numeral were landing on two mirror halves of one sectioned part. Arrowed lead lines touching the outer contour of the housing and the left end face of the sleeve identify the assembly and the removable unit as units, and leaving the lower housing band unnumbered removes the mirror-image pairing that made 10 read as a second housing part.

Numeral 28 moved off the left enlarged portion for the same reason: that block is what FIG. 2 designates 30, so 28 had to reach the piston as a body. An arrowed lead line on the lower outline at the junction of the middle and right portions touches the body rather than any one land, and it stays clear of the features FIG. 2 numbers.

The left rinse opening moved off the concentrate port station because a land that covers the port also spans the bore at that station, which blocked the rinse path the description and claim 15 require. Placing the opening immediately right of the left enlarged portion gives its inner mouth an open path into the bore while keeping the disclosed direction toward the concentrate port.

I also moved FIG. 2's unnumbered lower openings to that same station, which the review did not raise. The two sections show the piston at nearly the same place, so leaving FIG. 2's opening at the old station would have put one physical opening at two axial stations across the sheets, which is the class of defect an earlier pass had already been asked to cure.

The description edit was a straight deletion. Nothing in the disclosure limits the axial extent of the sleeve-to-housing spacing, and claim 1 and the surrounding text already recite the annular rinse channel between the sleeve outer surface and the housing inner surface, so the qualifier carried no work and no support.

data.summary: All eight findings are fixed, seven inside figures/ and one in the description. The two critical disclosure-fidelity items: the carrier-liquid admission port no longer opens into the annulus that FIG. 3 designates the annular rinse channel, its outer mouth being broken off at a conventional break line within the lower sleeve band in FIG. 2, with the matching break added to the covered lower opening in FIG. 3, so no feed connection between the admission path and the rinse channel is asserted; and the flush poppet no longer has a permanent linkage to the follower pin, the closure element now carrying a plain stem whose free end is abutted by the pin in this view, which matches the description's statement that the pin reaches the poppet and opens it near the end of the return stroke. The four major items: FIG. 1 numeral 10 now reaches the assembly by an arrowed lead line touching the outer contour of the housing at the upper right while 12 takes the upper housing wall band and the lower band is left unnumbered; numeral 64 now touches the left end face of the sleeve where it stands in the left mouth of the housing, clear of the bands targeted by 18; the annular rinse channel in FIG. 3 is open at the left toward the inlet end of the housing with its right end closed by the sleeve meeting the housing wall, so the supply path recited in the description, the summary and claim 1 is traceable in the figure; and "over part of its length" is deleted from the sleeve spacing sentence in the detailed description. The two minor items: the left radial rinse opening in FIG. 3 now lies immediately right of the left enlarged portion with its inner mouth open to the bore and directed toward the concentrate port, so nothing covers it; and numeral 28 reaches the piston as a whole by an arrowed lead line touching its lower outline where the middle portion meets the right enlarged portion, instead of landing on the block that FIG. 2 numbers 30. FIG. 2's unnumbered lower openings moved to the same axial station the FIG. 3 fix uses, so one opening is not drawn at two stations across the two sections. All four briefs were retrimmed to stay under the 2800 character cap; the space came from redundant phrasing such as a repeated statement that the stubs end inside the drawing area, not from geometry or relationships.
reasoning: The two critical items were both flow-topology assertions, and each was cured by removing the assertion rather than by adding structure. Showing the admission port's outer mouth broken off leaves the figure silent on where the port draws from, which is where the disclosure is silent, and it prevents the drawing from implying that the rinse channel feeds the metering charge, a path that would sit under the control of the flush poppet and would change what the valve does.

The poppet stem was the more consequential of the two. A permanent stem linkage would mean the follower pin governs the poppet throughout every stroke, which contradicts the disclosed timing that the poppet is normally closed and is opened near the end of the return stroke, and that timing is what claim 1 rests on. Making the stem a member of the poppet that the pin merely abuts in this one view keeps the depicted contact without asserting a permanent connection.

The rinse channel had to be opened at the inlet end rather than left closed at both ends, because the description, the summary and claim 1 all recite carrier liquid flowing through the channel, and the inlet is the only carrier-liquid source the disclosure gives. Closing the right end at the sleeve-to-housing junction keeps the single ordered route of channel, rinse openings, flush bypass, outlet, and does not reopen the permanent bypass that an earlier pass removed.

For numerals 10 and 12 and for 18 and 64, the problem was that a whole-assembly numeral and a component numeral were landing on two mirror halves of one sectioned part. Arrowed lead lines touching the outer contour of the housing and the left end face of the sleeve identify the assembly and the removable unit as units, and leaving the lower housing band unnumbered removes the mirror-image pairing that made 10 read as a second housing part.

Numeral 28 moved off the left enlarged portion for the same reason: that block is what FIG. 2 designates 30, so 28 had to reach the piston as a body. An arrowed lead line on the lower outline at the junction of the middle and right portions touches the body rather than any one land, and it stays clear of the features FIG. 2 numbers.

The left rinse opening moved off the concentrate port station because a land that covers the port also spans the bore at that station, which blocked the rinse path the description and claim 15 require. Placing the opening immediately right of the left enlarged portion gives its inner mouth an open path into the bore while keeping the disclosed direction toward the concentrate port.

I also moved FIG. 2's unnumbered lower openings to that same station, which the review did not raise. The two sections show the piston at nearly the same place, so leaving FIG. 2's opening at the old station would have put one physical opening at two axial stations across the sheets, which is the class of defect an earlier pass had already been asked to cure.

The description edit was a straight deletion. Nothing in the disclosure limits the axial extent of the sleeve-to-housing spacing, and claim 1 and the surrounding text already recite the annular rinse channel between the sleeve outer surface and the housing inner surface, so the qualifier carried no work and no support.

10

The source affirms both features simultaneously - the collar surrounds the sleeve inside the housing (it is read through a window in the housing) and the rinse channel lies between the sleeve and the housing - so the drawing must show the collar clear of the housing bore.
39	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-1.md, change the sleeve bullet to read "...spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it along its length", and change the ring bullet to "An unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length, standing clear of the housing wall so that the gap continues past it, its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end." As written the figure brief contradicts the claim language it must support.
41	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, change the bullet to begin: "Toward the right, downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage, a passage leads from the sleeve bore up through the upper sleeve band toward the outlet: the flush bypass."
