View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- An outer housing wall appears in section as upper and lower hatched bands, with the sleeve wall inside it as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward; between them is the bore.
- The clear gap between the sleeve bands and the outer housing bands is the annular rinse channel, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end of the housing at the left; no closure of either end of the gap is indicated.
- In the bore, in the left half, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion. A plain shaft extends leftward on the axis past the sleeve's left end, and a short pin projects from the shaft.

- A further opening through the lower sleeve band at the right portion of the piston is covered by it, its outer mouth broken off within the band; unnumbered.

# FIG. 1

View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched wall bands that run across most of the view, joined at the right by a hatched end wall. The interior between them is open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth, meeting the housing bore along a shallow saw-tooth interface indicating a thread. A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the body, out of the left end of the sleeve bore, and is broken off at a conventional break line short of the end cap.
- A short tubular stub projects leftward from the left end of the housing below the axis, clear of the end cap and the shaft, and opens into the interior: the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects rightward from the end wall at the right and opens into the interior: the outlet, shown schematically.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis, drawn as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it along its length.
- The sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry are drawn as one removable unit, the sleeve's left end standing within the left mouth of the housing short of the end cap; this unit is the cartridge.
- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, the plain shaft running leftward from it.
- An unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length, standing clear of the housing wall so that the gap continues past it, its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end.
- An unhatched panel of simple outline, shown schematically, is set into the upper housing wall band above the ring, the hatching stopping at its outline; it is the transparent window. On the ring beneath the panel a small plain patch shows.

Numerals on this sheet: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66.

Targets:

- 10: the assembly as a whole, by an arrowed lead line touching the outer contour of the housing at the upper right of the view.

- 14: the wall of the left axial stub.
- 16: the wall of the right axial stub.
- 18: the hatched upper band of the sleeve.
- 52: the interior of the unhatched panel.
- 64: the removable unit, by an arrowed lead line touching the left end face of the sleeve where it stands in the left mouth of the housing.
- 66: the hatched ring in the left mouth of the housing.

lines: The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

-FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

+FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62, the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.
The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

- A short tubular stub projects leftward from the left end of the housing below the axis, clear of the end cap and the shaft, and opens into the interior: the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects rightward from the end wall at the right and opens into the interior: the outlet, shown schematically.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis, drawn as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it along its length.
- The sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry are drawn as one removable unit, the sleeve's left end standing within the left mouth of the housing short of the end cap; this unit is the cartridge.
- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, the plain shaft running leftward from it.
- An unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length, standing clear of the housing wall so that the gap continues past it, its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end.
- An unhatched panel of simple outline, shown schematically, is set into the upper housing wall band above the ring, the hatching stopping at its outline; it is the transparent window. On the ring beneath the panel a small plain patch shows.

input.summary: All seven findings are fixed inside figures/, with one synchronizing edit to the description. The three critical FIG. 3 items: the invented poppet stem is gone, the flush poppet now being a plain closure element shown schematically adjacent the left end of the sleeve, at the position the follower pin reaches at the end of the return stroke, held open by that pin and connected to the flush bypass by a plain passage, with target 58 reading "the plain closure element held open by the follower pin"; the annular rinse channel is now the clear gap between the sleeve bands and the outer housing bands, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end at the left, with no closure of either end indicated, so no undisclosed flow boundary is asserted; and the two rinse openings are placed only at the axial station of the concentrate port and at that of the outlet-valve passage, with their relationship to the sealing lands and any direction of discharge expressly not indicated, which removes both the untraced station and the blocked jet. The major item: FIG. 1's clear gap now runs along the length of the sleeve and the unnumbered ring stands clear of the housing wall so the gap continues past it, so the collar no longer occupies the rinse annulus and the path from the inlet end to the rinse openings and the flush bypass is continuous. The three minor items: the flush bypass in FIG. 3 is now expressly downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage, matching claims 1 and 13; FIG. 4 names the left end, the end from which the piston rod enters, as the stepped end, with the shallow curved edge indicating the round section moved to the right end and target 46 reading "one of the three stepped faces at the left end of the collar"; and FIG. 1's window panel is now an unhatched panel of simple outline expressly shown schematically. The description edit is confined to the FIG. 3 recitation sentence, which now lists the two radial rinse openings 62 and the concentrate port 22 without stating that the figure shows a direction of discharge; the disclosed direction across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve remains in the following paragraph, in the summary and in claims 2 and 15. Every sheet's numeral list is unchanged, and the four briefs are 2763, 2777, 2789 and 2761 characters.
reasoning: The poppet fix was the one with real consequences for the drawing's coherence. A stem running from the bypass at the right to the pin outside the sleeve's left end would have to cross the sealed bore and the two-land piston, so the linkage could not exist in the depicted structure. Putting the closure element where the pin actually arrives at the end of the return stroke keeps the disclosed relationship, that the pin opens a normally closed poppet connected to the flush bypass, without inventing an actuating member or a route for it.

The rinse channel and the FIG. 1 ring had to be fixed together. Closing the channel's right end while the collar blocked the annulus at the left left the channel with neither a supply nor a discharge, which contradicts the description, the summary and claim 1. Leaving both ends unstated and standing the ring clear of the housing wall gives a continuous annulus from the inlet end through the rinse openings to the flush bypass, and it keeps both disclosed facts true at once: the collar surrounds the sleeve inside the housing, where a window can read it, and the rinse channel lies between the sleeve and the housing.

For the rinse openings I removed the axial station relative to the lands rather than moving it again. Two earlier passes moved that opening to cure a blocked path, and each new station was itself untraced. The source gives the number of openings and the surfaces they are directed across, nothing more, so stating only the two stations that are disclosed by reference to the port and the valve, and declining to fix any relationship to the lands or any jet direction, is the version that stays inside the disclosure.

The flush bypass wording mattered because the figure brief was contradicting the claim it has to support: claims 1 and 13 require the bypass to open downstream of the dose chamber, and the brief had it leading from the bore. Naming it downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage aligns the sheet with the claim without adding structure.

Naming the stepped end of the collar in FIG. 4 forced a second change in the same brief, since the first bullet had closed the left end with the curved edge that indicates the round section. I moved that edge to the right end rather than leave two incompatible statements about the left end, and updated target 46 to name the left end so the leader cannot land on the wrong end face.

The description edit was not requested, but the FIG. 3 recitation had asserted that the figure shows one rinse opening directed across the concentrate port, which is exactly what the brief now declines to indicate. Rather than reintroduce the direction into the drawing, I removed the claim about what the figure shows and left the disclosed direction where it belongs, in the body text and the dependent claims. Every numeral recited for the sheet is still recited, so the sheet list, the target list and the description paragraph still agree.

Length had to be managed again, since the poppet fix added a bullet. The space came from redundant phrasing in the same briefs, such as repeating 'shown schematically' twice in one sentence and naming the view twice in one target, not from geometry, relationships or the hedges that cure the untraced items.

The claimed combination is untouched this turn. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and the port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- An outer housing wall appears in section as upper and lower hatched bands, with the sleeve wall inside it as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward; between them is the bore.
- The clear gap between the sleeve bands and the outer housing bands is the annular rinse channel, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end at the left; no closure of either end of the gap is indicated.
- In the bore, in the left half, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion. A plain shaft extends leftward on the axis past the sleeve's left end, with a short pin projecting from it.
- Thin flexible projections extend from the left portion into contact with the upper and lower bore walls: the flexible lip, shown schematically without flare direction.
- An opening through the upper sleeve band, covered by the left portion, is the concentrate port, with a short stub rising from it, broken off in the view.
- Right of the piston a passage leads up through the upper sleeve band, with a plain closure element across it: the one-way outlet valve, unnumbered.
- Toward the right, downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage, a passage leads from the sleeve bore up through the upper sleeve band toward the outlet: the flush bypass.
- Adjacent the left end of the sleeve, at the position reached by the follower pin at the end of the return stroke, a plain closure element shown schematically is the flush poppet, held open by the pin and connected to the flush bypass by a plain passage.
- Two openings through the lower sleeve band connect the rinse channel to the bore, shown schematically: one at the axial station of the concentrate port and one at that of the outlet-valve passage. Their relationship to the sealing lands and any direction of discharge are not indicated.
- A further opening through the lower sleeve band at the right portion of the piston is covered by it, its outer mouth broken off within the band; unnumbered.

Numerals on this sheet: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62.

Targets:

- 22: interior of the upper opening at the left.
- 26: interior of the bypass passage.
- 28: the piston as a whole, by an arrowed lead line touching its lower outline where the middle and right portions meet.
- 44: the short pin on the shaft.
- 56: the flexible projection at the upper bore wall.
- 58: the plain closure element held open by the follower pin.
- 60: the clear gap between the lower bands.
- 62: the left lower opening.

# FIG. 1

View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched wall bands that run across most of the view, joined at the right by a hatched end wall. The interior between them is open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth, meeting the housing bore along a shallow saw-tooth interface indicating a thread. A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the body, out of the left end of the sleeve bore, and is broken off at a conventional break line short of the end cap.
- A short tubular stub projects leftward from the left end of the housing below the axis, clear of the end cap and the shaft, and opens into the interior: the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects rightward from the end wall at the right and opens into the interior: the outlet, shown schematically.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis, drawn as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it along its length.
- The sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry are drawn as one removable unit, the sleeve's left end standing within the left mouth of the housing short of the end cap; this unit is the cartridge.
- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, the plain shaft running leftward from it.
- An unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length, standing clear of the housing wall so that the gap continues past it, its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end.
- An unhatched panel of simple outline, shown schematically, is set into the upper housing wall band above the ring, the hatching stopping at its outline; it is the transparent window. On the ring beneath the panel a small plain patch shows.

Numerals on this sheet: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66.

Targets:

- 10: the assembly as a whole, by an arrowed lead line touching the outer contour of the housing at the upper right.
- 12: the hatched upper housing wall band.
- 14: the wall of the left axial stub.
- 16: the wall of the right axial stub.
- 18: the hatched upper band of the sleeve.
- 52: the interior of the unhatched panel.
- 64: the removable unit, by an arrowed lead line touching the left end face of the sleeve in the housing's left mouth.
- 66: the hatched ring in the left mouth of the housing.

input.summary: All three findings are fixed, and all three fixes are confined to the figure briefs; no application text needed to change. FIG. 4 no longer assigns the three axial stop faces to a named end of the collar and no longer states what abuts them: one end of the collar is stepped, its end face divided into three faces at three different axial positions shown schematically, with the arrangement order and the abutting part expressly not indicated. Target 46 follows, reading "one of the three stepped faces at the stepped end of the collar", and the shallow curved edge that indicates the round section is now placed at the end opposite the stepped end, so the brief names no absolute end for the stop faces while still describing a single coherent body. FIG. 3's rinse openings are now placed one adjacent the concentrate port and one adjacent the outlet-valve passage, each opening into the bore at a station clear of the sealing lands in the position shown, with any direction of discharge not indicated; that removes both the blocked path, since no opening now sits at the station the upstream sealing land covers, and the self-contradiction between a fixed station and a disclaimer about the lands. FIG. 1's inlet is now a short tubular stub projecting from the left end of the housing and opening into the interior, shown schematically, with the radial offset and its relation to the end cap and the shaft deleted; the two stub targets were reworded to name the stub at the left end and the stub at the right end so they no longer describe the stubs as axial after that change. The outlet sentence, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions, the detailed description and the claims are untouched, every sheet's numeral list is unchanged, and all four briefs remain under the 2800 character cap at 2742, 2777, 2788 and 2722 characters.
reasoning: All three findings were untraced statements rather than missing structure, so each was cured by deletion plus an express statement that the point is not indicated. That keeps the disclosed parts on the sheets, the three stop faces, the two rinse openings and the inlet, while leaving the drawing silent exactly where the disclosure is silent.

The stop-face fix had a knock-on inside the same brief. The first bullet had put the curved edge that indicates the round section at the right end, which was only there because the previous pass had named the left end as stepped. Leaving it absolute would have re-implied which end carries the stop faces, so I made it relative to the stepped end. The brief still describes one determinate body, and no absolute end is named for a functional face.

For the rinse openings I moved from naming an axial station to naming a neighbour port plus a clearance condition. Stating that each opening lies adjacent its port and opens into the bore clear of the sealing lands in the position shown gives the renderer enough to place them, keeps the rinse path open at the moment the description and claim 1 recite it flowing, and stops the brief from fixing a relationship to the lands that the source never gives.

The inlet fix removes a radial position that had been carried since the first draft. The disclosure places the inlet only at one axial end of the cylindrical housing, so the stub's height relative to the axis, the end cap and the piston rod was drafter's choice; a generic stub at that end shows the disclosed feature without asserting where it sits radially.

I reworded the two stub targets, which the review did not raise, because the geometry no longer describes either stub as axial. Leaving targets that named an axial stub would have pointed at a description the brief had stopped making, which is the kind of stale cross-reference an earlier pass was already asked to clear.

The application text was left alone deliberately. Claims 7 and 18 recite three selectable axial stop faces carried by the index collar at different axial positions, and the detailed description matches; both are already end-neutral and say nothing about what abuts the faces, so the drawings were the only place the untraced matter lived.

Nothing this turn touched the claimed combination. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and the port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. The rinse-opening fix supports that ground rather than disturbing it, since it keeps the rinse path open in the drawing at the instant claim 1 recites carrier liquid flowing through the annular rinse channel, through the rinse opening and through the flush bypass to the outlet. The dependent ladder is unchanged: the two directed rinse openings in claims 2 and 15, the flexible lip, the closed-port rinse interval, the ordered land and port geometry, the index collar with its three stop faces, detent and window, and the cartridge with threaded end cap.

# FIG. 3

View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. The index collar and the parts it carries are omitted from this view for clarity. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- An outer housing wall appears in section as upper and lower hatched bands, with the sleeve wall inside it as hatched bands spaced inward; between them is the bore.
- The clear gap between the sleeve bands and the outer bands is the annular rinse channel, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end at the left; no closure of either end is indicated.
- In the bore, in the left half, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, with a plain shaft extending leftward on the axis past the sleeve's left end and a short pin projecting from that shaft.
- Thin flexible projections extend from the left portion into contact with the upper and lower bore walls: the flexible lip, shown schematically without flare direction.
- An opening through the upper sleeve band, covered by the left portion, is the concentrate port, with a short stub rising from it, broken off.
- Right of the piston a passage leads up through the upper sleeve band, with a plain closure element across it: the one-way outlet valve, unnumbered.
- Toward the right, downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage, a passage leads from the sleeve bore up through the upper band toward the outlet: the flush bypass.
- Adjacent the left end of the sleeve, where the follower pin reaches at the end of the return stroke, a plain closure element shown schematically is the flush poppet, held open by the pin and connected to the flush bypass by a plain passage.
- Two openings through the lower sleeve band connect the rinse channel to the bore, shown schematically: one adjacent the concentrate port and one adjacent the outlet-valve passage, each opening clear of the sealing lands in the position shown. Any direction of discharge is not indicated.
- A further opening through the lower sleeve band at the right portion of the piston is covered by it, its outer mouth broken off within the band; unnumbered.

input.summary: All three findings are fixed, and all three fixes stay inside figures/; no application text changed. In FIG. 2 the fill-position view no longer asserts an open path from the carrier-liquid gap into the dose chamber: the two lower openings now have their outer mouths broken off at a conventional break line within the band, so what they open into is not indicated, which is the same convention the brief already uses for the carrier-liquid admission port. In FIG. 4 the piston rod and the follower pin are now treated like the tube they lie inside, the rod's length within the collar and the pin's hidden length being drawn as hidden outlines in broken line, so one side view no longer mixes two line conventions for parts behind the same surface. In FIG. 3 the view line now states that the index collar and the parts it carries are omitted from that view for clarity, so the clear annulus in FIG. 3 no longer reads as a structural difference from the ring shown in FIG. 1 and the collar shown in FIG. 4. Adding those passages pushed all three briefs over the 2800 character cap, so I recovered the space from redundant phrasing in the same files: repeated "sleeve band" and "shown schematically" qualifiers, a restated reference to the recess broken into the outline, "This is the ..." constructions folded into colons, and two targets that named a band the sheet has only one of. Every sheet's numeral list, the four captions in the Brief Description, the numeral table, the detailed description and the claims are unchanged, and the four briefs now measure 2742, 2753, 2794 and 2788 characters.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 item was the one that mattered to the invention. As written the fill-position sheet showed carrier liquid able to reach the dose chamber at the same station where the concentrate port stood open to it, which is exactly the communication the description, the summary and claim 1 say the land and port geometry prevents. Breaking off the outer mouths leaves the openings on the sheet, since they are disclosed, while the figure stops asserting anything about the path they belong to in a position the source never describes them in.

I used the break-off convention rather than moving the openings again. Their axial station has already been moved twice in earlier passes to cure a blocked or open path, and each new station was itself untraced; withdrawing the flow-boundary assertion is the fix that does not invent a third position.

The FIG. 4 fix is a line-convention correction, not a geometry change. A side view has to treat everything behind the collar surface the same way, so the rod and the pin now follow the tube into broken line. Targets 36 and 44 were left alone: the rod is still identified where it enters the view clear of the collar, and the pin is still the short radial projection at the shaft end, so both leaders still land on the intended parts.

For FIG. 3 the choice was between drawing the collar into an already crowded enlarged section and stating the omission. Stating it is the conventional and the smaller change: FIG. 4 exists precisely to carry the collar and its eight numerals, and adding the collar to FIG. 3 would have introduced structure into a sheet whose eight numerals are already at the per-sheet maximum.

Length was the binding constraint this turn, since every fix added text. I took the space from wording that repeats what the brief already establishes rather than from geometry, relationships or the hedges that cure untraced matter, so the substance of each sheet is intact and the three new passages are the only material changes.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none may be invented; the brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art behind this draft may be incomplete and the independent claims should be re-tested against any later search. The claimed combination is untouched. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and the port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. The FIG. 2 fix defends the first of those directly: the drawings no longer depict, in the fill position, any route by which the carrier-liquid side could reach the open concentrate port, which is the property the specification explains at length and from which a later argument about geometric rather than commanded isolation would be built. The dependent ladder is unchanged: the two directed rinse openings in claims 2 and 15, the flexible lip, the closed-port rinse interval, the express axial ordering of land faces and port edges, the index collar with its three stop faces, detent and window, and the cartridge with threaded end cap.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after the concentrate port 22 has been closed does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. The port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62, the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

input.summary: All nine findings are fixed. In the detailed description, the sentence assigning closure of the concentrate port to the upstream sealing land is gone, the passage now reading that only after the concentrate port has been closed does continued travel carry the downstream sealing land clear of the carrier-liquid admission port, and the enumerated slow, interrupted and part-way-reversed stroke conditions are gone, leaving the general statement that the port which must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens. In FIG. 3 the concentrate port is covered by the piston rather than by the left portion, the one-way outlet valve passage no longer carries a position relative to the piston, and the flush bypass is located only downstream of the dose chamber. In FIG. 2 the outlet valve passage no longer carries a position relative to the downstream sealing land, the rinse openings are removed from the fill-position view in favour of a single further opening whose outer mouth is broken off so that what it opens into is not indicated, and the clause placing a further passage right of the outlet-valve passage is deleted; the two rinse openings remain shown and numbered 62 in FIG. 3, at the return-stroke position where the source requires them to be open. Both FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 now close their geometry with a statement that the band in which each port, opening and passage is drawn is a section-plane convention only and that no circumferential relationship between them is intended. In FIG. 1 the inlet stub is offset from the axis and clear of the end cap ring and of the shaft, so the three features at that end no longer read as occupying the same place. In FIG. 4 the right end of the collar, through which the unnumbered tube enters, carries the shallow curved edge and the left end is stepped, with target 46 naming the left end, while the sentence declining to indicate the circumferential arrangement and the abutting part is retained. Space for the added sentences came from redundant phrasing in the same briefs; the numeral table, the per-sheet numeral lists, the Brief Description captions and the claims are unchanged, and the four briefs measure 2793, 2683, 2785 and 2787 characters.
reasoning: The two description edits were deletions of drafted inference. Removing the sentence that named the upstream land as the one shutting the concentrate port also removes the implied direction of the metering stroke, and with it the chain that made the axial ordering read as putting the downstream land between the admission port and the outlet valve. The remaining text recites only the disclosed sequence: concentrate port closed before the admission port is uncovered, then carrier liquid entering behind the measured volume and expelling it through the one-way outlet valve.

The same deletion resolves the expulsion-path contradiction without touching claim 1 or claim 5. Claim 5 recites the axial positioning of the land faces relative to the port edges in functional terms and never names which land arrives at which port, so nothing in the claims had to move once the description stopped fixing the choice.

Dropping the relative axial position of the outlet valve from both briefs was the fix that mattered most for coherence, because that position, not the disclosure, was what put a sealing land between the admitted carrier liquid and the valve it must reach. Stating only that the passage leads from the dose chamber up through the band toward the outlet keeps the disclosed function and leaves the ordering unasserted.

For the fill-position sheet I removed the rinse openings rather than moving them yet again. Their station has been relocated in three earlier passes, and each new station either blocked the flush path or opened the carrier side to the concentrate port. FIG. 3 is the view the source ties them to, since that is the position at which the poppet is held open, so the openings stay numbered there and FIG. 2 makes no assertion about them at all.

The circumferential convention sentence goes in the briefs only. A longitudinal section has to draw each port in one wall band, so the choice is forced by the view rather than disclosed, and the application text contains no orientation language at all. Saying so inside the brief keeps the forced choice from reading as an assertion that the ports are opposed, without putting any orientation into the specification.

On FIG. 1 I restored the inlet stub's offset, which an earlier pass had removed as untraced, because the end cap and the rod exit are both at that end and a renderer reading the bullet without the offset would stack all three in one place. The offset is a placement convention inside the brief; the description continues to recite only an inlet at one axial end.

On FIG. 4 the stepped end had to be named absolutely for numeral 46 to have a determinate target, and naming the right end as the one the tube enters supplies the other end at the same time. What stays unstated is the part the stop faces abut and their circumferential order, which is where the source is silent.

Every added sentence cost characters against the 2800 cap, so I trimmed wording that repeats what the brief already establishes: duplicated band names, a second 'shown schematically' in the same bullet, and two leader descriptions that specified more of the endpoint than was needed to identify the part.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer

# FIG. 1

View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched wall bands joined at the right by a hatched end wall. The interior between them is open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth, meeting the housing bore along a shallow saw-tooth interface indicating a thread. A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the body out of the sleeve bore and is broken off at a conventional break line.
- A short tubular stub projects leftward from the housing at its left end and opens into the interior: the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects rightward from the end wall at the right: the outlet, shown schematically.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it along its length.
- The sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry are drawn as one removable unit, the sleeve's left end standing within the left mouth of the housing and meeting the inner face of the end cap ring that retains it; this unit is the cartridge.
- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, with the plain shaft running leftward.
- An unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length, its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end.
- An unhatched panel of simple outline, shown schematically, is set into the upper housing wall band above the ring, the hatching stopping at its outline: the transparent window. On the ring beneath it a small plain patch shows.
- The radial clearance drawn between the ring and the housing wall, and the position of the inlet stub within the left end, are drawing conventions only: no flow path past the ring, and no radial position of or relationship between the inlet, the end cap ring and the shaft, is intended.

Numerals on this sheet: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66.

Targets:

- 10: the assembly as a whole, by an arrowed lead line touching the housing's outer contour at the upper right.
- 12: the hatched upper housing wall band.

input.summary: All five findings are fixed, all inside figures/; no application text needed to change. FIG. 1 now has the cartridge's sleeve end standing in the left mouth of the housing and meeting the inner face of the end cap ring that retains it, so the retention joint is a contact rather than a gap, and the piston rod bullet no longer says the shaft is broken off short of the end cap, which would have squeezed the rod into a zero-length space at that joint. The FIG. 1 ring bullet now states only that the unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length with its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end, and the inlet bullet is back to a generic stub projecting leftward from the housing at its left end; a single closing sentence records that the radial clearance drawn between the ring and the housing wall, and the position of the inlet stub within the left end, are drawing conventions only, with no flow path past the ring and no radial position of or relationship between the inlet, the end cap ring and the shaft intended. FIG. 4's cam groove is now a narrow band wrapping the collar body with its outline in broken line in the same manner as the hidden tube and rod, and the brief states that the surface of the collar on which the groove is formed, and its hand and pitch, are not indicated; the follower pin still has its outer end within that band. The extra unidentified opening is deleted from FIG. 2, leaving the concentrate port, the carrier-liquid admission port and the outlet-valve passage on that sheet, with the two radial rinse openings shown and numbered 62 in FIG. 3 at the return-stroke position. Because three of the fixes add text, I trimmed redundant phrasing in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4, including a duplicated statement about the interior of the housing, two leader descriptions that named the housing twice, and repeated broken-line qualifiers, so the four briefs measure 2787, 2490, 2785 and 2789 characters. The numeral table, the per-sheet numeral lists, the Brief Description captions, the detailed description and the claims are unchanged.
reasoning: The end cap joint was the fix that most affected the drawing's fidelity to the disclosure. A cap drawn short of the cartridge cannot retain it, which is the one relationship the source states about that joint, so closing the gap makes the sheet agree with the disclosed function rather than with a drafter's clearance.

That change forced a second edit in the same bullet: the rod had been broken off short of the end cap, which only made sense while a gap existed there. Dropping the phrase leaves the break line doing what a break line does, asserting nothing about where the rod goes, and avoids stating that the rod occupies a space the cartridge now fills.

For the cam groove I moved the whole feature into broken line and said in terms that the surface carrying it is not indicated. The earlier hedge covered only hand and pitch, which left the brief asserting an outer-surface or through-wall cam reached by a pin on an internal rod. Putting the groove in the same hidden-line treatment as the tube and the rod keeps the disclosed engagement between groove and pin visible without choosing a radial position for it.

The collar clearance and the inlet position both became labelled conventions rather than stated geometry, and I combined them into one closing sentence instead of two. The substance is that neither the flow past the collar nor the inlet's radial position is intended, which is exactly where the source is silent; a single sentence says both and costs fewer characters against the length cap.

Deleting the unidentified FIG. 2 opening was the cleanest resolution because every opening the source discloses is already drawn and numbered somewhere: the concentrate port and the admission port on FIG. 2, the flush bypass and the two rinse openings on FIG. 3. An opening that answers to no disclosed part cannot be traced, and its presence also left the two sections showing different counts through the same wall.

The rinse openings stay off the fill-position sheet, which is where earlier passes landed after their station proved untraceable in that position. FIG. 3 is the view the source ties them to, since that is the position at which the poppet is held open and the rinse flows.
Length was again the binding constraint, so the trims came from wording that repeats what a brief already establishes rather than from geometry or from the hedges that cure the untraced items.

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Scope. The authority is a single USER passage, identical in input/disclosure.md and input/conversation.md (five paragraphs describing the valve, the piston/land/port ordering, the index collar, the rinse sequence and the cartridge). input/brief.md was used only for formalities: title (matches draft/01 exactly), applicant/inventor, "Not applicable." in draft/02 and draft/03, the apparatus+method claim classes, the no-means-plus-function instruction, and the preserved terminology list (metering sleeve, dose chamber, flush bypass, index collar, flush poppet, annular rinse channel - all present and used consistently). prior_art/INDEX.md lists no documents, so the Background correctly contains no citations, and its prior-art characterizations were not traced to the inventor.
4	
5	Ledger result. Every limitation of claims 1-20 traces to an exact source sentence. Claim 1 and claim 13 map element-for-element: housing with inlet and outlet; metering sleeve fixed within the housing defining dose chamber, concentrate port, carrier-liquid admission port and a flush bypass opening downstream of the dose chamber; annular rinse channel between the sleeve's outer surface and the housing's inner surface; rinse opening through the sleeve; piston slidable between fill and discharge positions with two axially spaced sealing lands joined by a reduced-diameter waist; piston rod carrying a follower pin; one-way outlet valve; normally closed flush poppet; fill-position isolation; the close-before-uncover ordering with carrier liquid entering behind the measured volume; and the follower-pin-opened flush closing before the waist reconnects the port. Dependents 2-12 and 14-20 likewise trace (two rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the outlet valve; flexible lip on the upstream land wiping first; port closed throughout the rinse interval; axial ordering of land faces and port edges; collar with helical cam groove indexed one increment per full stroke; three axial stop faces setting three dose volumes; spring-biased detent in one of three recesses; window showing one of three dose setting numerals associated with the governing stop face; cartridge containing piston, sleeve, one-way outlet valve and flush poppet, retained by a threaded end cap, withdrawn without disturbing the inlet and outlet connections; cylindrical housing with inlet and outlet at opposite axial ends). # FIG. 1

View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched wall bands joined at the right by a hatched end wall, the interior between them open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth, its interface with the housing bore drawn as a shallow saw-tooth indicating a thread. A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the body out of the sleeve bore and is broken off at a conventional break line.
- A short tubular stub projects leftward from the housing at its left end and opens into the interior: the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects rightward from the end wall: the outlet, shown schematically.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it, interrupted only where the unnumbered ring described below surrounds the sleeve.
- The sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry are drawn as one removable unit, the sleeve's left end standing in the left mouth and meeting the inner face of the end cap ring that retains it: the cartridge.
- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, the plain shaft running leftward.
- An unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length, its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end.
- An unhatched panel of simple outline, shown schematically, is set into the upper housing wall band above that ring, the hatching stopping at its outline: the transparent window. On the ring beneath it a small patch shows.
- The radial clearance drawn between the unnumbered ring and the housing wall is a drawing convention only; no flow path past that ring is intended. Where the inlet stub is drawn within the left end is likewise a convention only; no radial position of, or relationship between, the inlet, the end cap ring and the shaft is intended.

- 66: the hatched ring in the left mouth.

- 10
- 12
- 14
- 16
- 18
- 52
- 64
- 66

# FIG. 1

View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched wall bands joined at the right by a hatched end wall, the interior between them open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth, its interface with the housing bore drawn as a shallow saw-tooth indicating a thread. A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the body out of the sleeve bore and is broken off at a conventional break line.
- A short tubular stub projects leftward from the housing at its left end and opens into the interior: the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects rightward from the end wall: the outlet, shown schematically.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it, interrupted only where the unnumbered ring described below surrounds the sleeve.

- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, the plain shaft running leftward.
- An unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length, its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end.
- An unhatched panel of simple outline, shown schematically, is set into the upper housing wall band above that ring, the hatching stopping at its outline: the transparent window. On the ring beneath it a small patch shows.
- The radial clearance drawn between the unnumbered ring and the housing wall is a drawing convention only; no flow path past that ring is intended. input.summary: All five findings are fixed inside figures/; no application text needed to change. FIG. 4 no longer says which end of the collar carries the three axial stop faces or that the end face is stepped: one end is drawn with its end face divided into three faces at three different axial positions, shown schematically, and the brief states that which end carries the faces, the order in which they are arranged about the collar, and the part that abuts them are not indicated; target 46 follows, reading "one of the three faces at the divided end of the collar". FIG. 3 now names the further opening through the lower band at the right portion of the piston as the carrier-liquid admission port, unnumbered in that view, with its outer mouth broken off at a break line within the band, so no opening on that sheet is left unidentified and numeral 24 stays on FIG. 2 alone. FIG. 2 now carries an express omission note that the two radial rinse openings shown in FIG. 3 are omitted from the fill-position view for clarity, which matches the omission note FIG. 3 already carries for the index collar and removes the impression that the two sections show different structures. FIG. 1's sleeve bullet now says the clear gap is interrupted only where the unnumbered ring described below surrounds the sleeve, so the two bullets no longer give the renderer contradictory instructions for the same annulus. FIG. 1's closing convention bullet is split into two sentences, the first naming the unnumbered ring surrounding the sleeve for the radial clearance and the no-flow-path statement, the second naming the inlet stub position and stating that no radial position of or relationship between the inlet, the end cap ring and the shaft is intended, so the two rings on that sheet can no longer be confused and the no-flow-path statement cannot attach to the retention joint. Space for the added sentences came from redundant phrasing in the same briefs, chiefly repeated uses of "sleeve band", "housing wall band" and "plain" where the sheet has only one such band, and from three leader descriptions that named a part twice. The numeral table, the per-sheet numeral lists, the Brief Description captions, the detailed description and the claims are unchanged, and the four briefs measure 2795, 2569, 2790 and 2795 characters.
reasoning: The stop-face fix follows the pattern the same brief already uses twice, for the inlet stub position and for the surface carrying the cam groove: keep the depiction the renderer needs, and say in terms which part of it is convention. Naming the divided end in target 46 rather than the left end keeps the leader determinate without reintroducing the end designation the source does not support.

Naming the FIG. 3 opening was the right cure rather than deleting it, because FIG. 2 draws the same feature at the same station and names it the carrier-liquid admission port. Deleting it would have made the sections disagree about a disclosed port; naming it and marking it unnumbered here keeps numeral 24 meaning one thing on one sheet.

The FIG. 2 omission note and the FIG. 3 collar omission note now do the same work from opposite directions. Both sheets are longitudinal sections of the same metering portion, so where one view leaves out a part the other shows, the brief has to say so, otherwise the pair reads as two different structures rather than one structure drawn twice.

The FIG. 1 gap wording was a straight renderer conflict: a clear gap along the whole length cannot coexist with a ring occupying part of that annulus. Qualifying the gap resolves it without saying anything about flow, which is where the source is silent and where the existing convention label already speaks.

Splitting the closing convention sentence mattered more than it looks. With the end cap introduced as a short hatched ring and the collar as an unnumbered ring, an unqualified reference to the ring could have attached the no-flow-path disclaimer to the retention joint, which is the one relationship at that joint the source does affirm. Naming each ring puts the disclaimer where it belongs.

Every fix added text against the length cap, so the trims came from wording that repeats what the brief already establishes, band names the sheet has only one of and leader endpoints described in more words than the part needs, rather than from geometry, relationships or the hedges that cure the untraced items.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or

input.summary: Both findings are fixed, and both fixes are confined to figures/FIG-1.md; no application text changed. The undisclosed flow boundary at the index collar is gone: the sleeve bullet now ends at a clear gap visible above and below the sleeve, with no statement that the gap is interrupted, and the closing convention bullet no longer says that no flow path past the ring is intended, so it now covers only the inlet stub position and states that no radial position of, or relationship between, the inlet, the end cap ring and the shaft is intended. In its place the ring bullet carries the neutral statement that no relationship between that ring and the gap between the sleeve and the housing is indicated, which leaves the drawing silent where the disclosure is silent and no longer cuts off the rinse supply that the description, FIG. 3 and claim 1 require to reach the annular rinse channel from the inlet. The collision between the ring and the end cap is also resolved: the cartridge bullet now reads that the sleeve stands in the left mouth and is retained there by the end cap ring, asserting no contact face, and the ring bullet no longer places the ring's left part beyond the sleeve's left end, so nothing is drawn into the space the cap occupies. Removing the two disclaimed sentences left FIG. 1 well under the length cap, so no other trimming was needed. The numeral table, the per-sheet numeral lists, the Brief Description captions, the detailed description, the claims and the other three briefs are unchanged, and the four sheets measure 2573, 2569, 2790 and 2795 characters.
reasoning: The flow-boundary statement had to go rather than be reworded, because it was doing real damage in two directions: it asserted a sealing or blocking relationship the inventor never described, and it closed the only route by which carrier liquid can reach the annular rinse channel, which the description, FIG. 3 and claim 1 all depend on. Deleting the interruption and the no-flow-path sentence restores a continuous annulus without asserting anything about how the collar sits in it.

Replacing them with a statement that no relationship between the ring and the gap is indicated keeps the sheet honest in both directions. It neither claims clearance nor claims a seal, which matches a source that places the collar around the sleeve and the channel between the sleeve and the housing without reconciling them.

The cartridge and ring collision came from an earlier fix that closed the retention joint by naming a contact face. Retention is disclosed; contact at a particular face is not. Saying the sleeve stands in the left mouth and is retained there by the end cap ring keeps the disclosed function, drops the untraced contact, and removes the geometric impossibility of a cap bearing on the sleeve end face while a larger ring passes through the same space.

I also dropped the clause putting the ring's left part beyond the sleeve's left end. It had been added in an earlier round to keep the follower pin at one station across sheets, but FIG. 4 already places the collar extending leftward beyond the tube's left end, so the relationship survives where it is drawn and FIG. 1 no longer needs to assert a position that collides with the cap.
No compensating trims were required this turn: the two deleted sentences were longer than the one added, so FIG. 1 dropped to 2573 characters and the other three briefs were left untouched.

The claimed combination is unchanged. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and the port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. This turn's edits protect the second of those directly: with the flow boundary at the collar removed, the drawings again show carrier liquid able to reach the annular rinse channel from the inlet, pass the rinse openings and leave through the flush bypass, which is the path claim 1 recites and the path the specification explains as making the rinse an unavoidable part of the same stroke. The dependent ladder is untouched: the two directed rinse openings in claims 2 and 15, the flexible lip, the closed-port rinse interval, the express axial ordering of land faces and port edges, the index collar with its cam groove, three stop faces, detent and window, and the cartridge with threaded end cap in claims 10, 11 and 20.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.

# FIG. 3

View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. The index collar and the parts it carries are omitted from this view for clarity. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- An outer housing wall appears in section as upper and lower hatched bands, with the sleeve wall inside as hatched bands spaced inward; between them is the bore.
- The clear gap between the sleeve and outer bands is the annular rinse channel, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end; no closure of either end is indicated.
- In the bore, in the left half, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, with a plain shaft extending leftward past the sleeve's left end and a short pin on it.
- Thin flexible projections extend from the left portion into contact with the bore walls: the flexible lip, shown without flare direction.
- An opening through the upper band, covered by the piston, is the concentrate port, with a short stub rising from it, broken off.
- A passage leads up through the upper band, with a plain closure element across it: the one-way outlet valve, unnumbered.
- Toward the right, downstream of the dose chamber, a passage leads from the bore up through the upper band toward the outlet: the flush bypass.
- Adjacent the left end of the sleeve, where the follower pin reaches at the end of the return stroke, a plain closure element shown schematically is the flush poppet, held open by the pin and joined to the flush bypass by a plain passage.
- Two openings through the lower band connect the rinse channel to the bore: one adjacent the concentrate port and one adjacent the outlet-valve passage, each clear of the sealing lands in the position shown; any direction of discharge is not indicated.
- A further opening through the lower band at the right portion of the piston is covered by that portion, its outer mouth broken off at a break line within the band: the carrier-liquid admission port, unnumbered here.
- The band in which each port and passage is drawn is a section-plane convention only; no circumferential relationship between them is intended.

# FIG. 4

View: fragmentary side view of the index collar and the parts that set and retain the dose, collar axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The index collar is drawn as a cylindrical ring seen from the side in the middle of the drawing area: a long horizontal body, its right end, through which an unnumbered tube enters, drawn with a shallow curved edge indicating the round section. The tube's left end lies within the collar, the collar extending leftward beyond that end, its hidden outline in broken line.
- A helical cam groove is drawn as a narrow band that wraps around the collar body, its outline in broken line in the same manner as the hidden tube and rod, shown schematically; the surface of the collar on which the groove is formed, and its hand and pitch, are not indicated.
- A piston rod is drawn as a plain horizontal shaft entering the view from the left on the collar axis, its length within the collar drawn as a hidden outline in broken line like the tube, ending within the left part of the collar. A short follower pin projects radially from the end of the shaft, drawn in broken line, its outer end within the narrow band of the groove.
- One end of the collar is drawn with its end face divided into three faces at three different axial positions, shown schematically: the three axial stop faces. Which end of the collar carries the faces, the order in which the three faces are arranged about the collar, and the part that abuts them, are not indicated.
- Three detent recesses lie at one station along the collar's length, at three angular positions about it, shown as plain recesses: one broken into the outline and the other two in broken line on the curved surface.
- Adjacent the collar, a spring-biased detent is shown as a plain detent element seated in that recess, with a spring behind it broken off.
- Three dose setting numerals lie at one station along the collar's length, at three angular positions about it, drawn as small plain patches, the middle one full on the visible surface and the others curving toward the upper and lower silhouettes; shown schematically, they carry no drawing text.

Numerals on this sheet: 36, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54.
